label: Acts 16:1
text: He came to Derbe and Lystra: and behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believed; but his father was a Greek.

label: Acts 16:2
text: The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony about him.

label: Acts 16:3
text: Paul wanted to have him go out with him, and he took and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those parts; for they all knew that his father was a Greek.

label: Acts 16:4
text: As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered the decrees to them to keep which had been ordained by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem.

label: Acts 16:5
text: So the assemblies were strengthened in the faith, and increased in number daily.

label: Acts 16:6
text: When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.

label: Acts 16:7
text: When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them.

label: Acts 16:8
text: Passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas.

label: Acts 16:9
text: A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him, and saying, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.”

label: Acts 16:10
text: When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the Good News to them.

label: Acts 16:11
text: Setting sail therefore from Troas, we made a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis;

label: Acts 16:12
text: and from there to Philippi, which is a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, a Roman colony. We were staying some days in this city.

label: Acts 16:13
text: On the Sabbath day we went outside of the city by a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down, and spoke to the women who had come together.

label: Acts 16:14
text: A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us; whose heart the Lord opened to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.

label: Acts 16:15
text: When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and stay.” So she persuaded us.

label: Acts 16:16
text: As we were going to prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of divination met us, who brought her masters much gain by fortune telling.

label: Acts 16:17
text: Following Paul and us, she cried out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us a way of salvation!”

label: Acts 16:18
text:
She was doing this for many days.
But Paul, becoming greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It came out that very hour.

label: Acts 16:19
text: But when her masters saw that the hope of their gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas, and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers.

label: Acts 16:20
text: When they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men, being Jews, are agitating our city,

label: Acts 16:21
text: and advocate customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans.”

label: Acts 16:22
text: The multitude rose up together against them, and the magistrates tore their clothes from them, and commanded them to be beaten with rods.

label: Acts 16:23
text: When they had laid many stripes on them, they threw them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely,

label: Acts 16:24
text: who, having received such a command, threw them into the inner prison, and secured their feet in the stocks.

label: Acts 16:25
text: But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.

label: Acts 16:26
text: Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.

label: Acts 16:27
text: The jailer, being roused out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.

label: Acts 16:28
text: But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!”

label: Acts 16:29
text: He called for lights, sprang in, fell down trembling before Paul and Silas,

label: Acts 16:30
text: brought them out, and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”

label: Acts 16:31
text: They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.”

label: Acts 16:32
text: They spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house.

variants.reading: the word of God (theou) at Acts 16:32
variants.note: Sinaiticus's original hand and B (with pc) read theou (God); P45, P74, a corrected Sinaiticus, A, C, (D), E, Psi, 33, 1739 and the Byzantine text read kyriou (Lord), as printed in the WEB (fetched Wikipedia, Papyrus 45).

label: Acts 16:33
text: He took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes, and was immediately baptized, he and all his household.

label: Acts 16:34
text: He brought them up into his house, and set food before them, and rejoiced greatly, with all his household, having believed in God.

label: Acts 16:35
text: But when it was day, the magistrates sent the sergeants, saying, “Let those men go.”

label: Acts 16:36
text: The jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go; now therefore come out, and go in peace.”

label: Acts 16:37
text: But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, without a trial, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison! Do they now release us secretly? No, most certainly, but let them come themselves and bring us out!”

label: Acts 16:38
text: The sergeants reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans,

label: Acts 16:39
text: and they came and begged them. When they had brought them out, they asked them to depart from the city.

label: Acts 16:40
text: They went out of the prison, and entered into Lydia’s house. When they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them, and departed.

label: Paul (Saul of Tarsus)
note: First mention at Acts 7:58 as the young man at whose feet the witnesses laid their garments; later Acts chapters reuse this node.

label: Timothy of Lystra
note: Disciple from Lystra; son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1); circumcised by Paul and joined the journey (16:3). No source outside the New Testament names him.

label: Lydia of Thyatira
note: Seller of purple cloth from Thyatira, Paul's first European convert at Philippi (Acts 16:14-15); her house became the meeting place (16:40). No source outside the New Testament names her.

label: Derbe
modern_name: Kerti Hüyük, near Ekinözü, Karaman Province, Turkey

label: Iconium
note: City of Lycaonia/Phrygia; the brothers here also testified for Timothy (Acts 16:2).

label: Phrygia
note: Region of the west Anatolian plateau; traversed at Acts 16:6.

label: Galatia (region and Roman province)
note: Roman province from 25 BC, capital Ancyra; traversed at Acts 16:6.

label: Asia (Roman province)
note: Senatorian province of western Asia Minor, capital Pergamon, later Ephesus; entry forbidden at Acts 16:6.

label: Bithynia
note: Region of northwestern Asia Minor on the Black Sea; the attempted destination at Acts 16:7.

label: Mysia
note: Region in northwest Asia Minor, bounded by the Troad; passed at Acts 16:7-8.

label: Troas (Alexandria Troas)
note: Chief port of northwest Asia Minor, from which the second journey crossed to Macedonia (Acts 16:8-11).

label: Samothrace
note: Greek island in the northern Aegean; the first stop on the crossing from Troas (Acts 16:11).

label: Neapolis (Macedonia)
note: Philippi's harbor on the Via Egnatia; Paul's European landing place (Acts 16:11).

label: Philippi
modern_name: Filippoi, Eastern Macedonia and Thrace, Greece
note: City of eastern Macedonia and Roman colony; the second journey's first European church (Acts 16:12-40).

label: Thyatira
note: City in the Roman province of Asia, famous for its dyeing works and purple cloth trade; Lydia's home city (Acts 16:14).

label: The Gangites (Zygaktis) river outside Philippi
note: Riverside outside the gate where Paul found the place of prayer (Acts 16:13); the identification of the Gangites with any surviving stream is disputed.

label: Philippi — the excavated ancient city (UNESCO Archaeological Site of Philippi)
note: Inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2016; Roman forum, theatre and Latin inscriptions of the colony.

label: Via Egnatia (Roman road, Dyrrachium to Byzantium)
note: The great Roman road across Macedonia and Thrace; Neapolis and Philippi are stations on it.

label: Inscriptions of the dyers' guild and other guilds of Thyatira
note: Inscriptions found among the ruins of Thyatira relating to the guild of dyers; Thyatira has more recorded guilds (syntechiai) than any other contemporary city of the province of Asia.

label: Two Delian stelae recording benefactions to a proseuche (house of prayer)
note: Marble stelae of Samaritan 'Israelites on Delos who make offerings to hallowed Argarizein', recording Cretan donors' benefactions to a proseuche ('house of prayer').

label: Cicero, In Verres 2.5 (the Porcian-law oration: 'I am a Roman citizen')
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
note: The prosecution of Verres for scourging and crucifying Roman citizens in Sicily (73-70 BCE): 'It is a crime to bind a Roman citizen; to scourge him is a wickedness; to put him to death is almost parricide' (2.5.66); 'O Porcian law!' (2.5.63). Older editions number the same passage Book 5, chapters 161-170.

label: Mishnah Kiddushin 3:12 (the matrilineal principle: the offspring is like her)
author: Judah the Prince (compiler)
note: Where a woman cannot join in betrothal with a man or with others, the offspring is like her: 'He is not considered his father's son at all, but has the same status as his mother.' Later redaction; may not state the practice of the 40s CE exactly.

label: Wikipedia: Delos (the Samaritan proseuche stelae)
title: Wikipedia: Delos (the Samaritan proseuche stelae)
excerpt: Two marble stelae dated on paleographic grounds to c. 250–175 BCE and c. 150–50 BCE, record benefactions by Cretan donors to a proseuche ("house of prayer"). In the inscriptions, the community identified itself as " Israelites on Delos who make offerings to hallowed Argarizein "

label: Timothy, a disciple at Lystra, son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father
statement: A disciple named Timothy was at Lystra: the son of a Jewish woman who believed, but his father was a Greek.

label: The brothers at Lystra and Iconium gave Timothy a good testimony
statement: The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave Timothy a good testimony.
note: Both cities already had Christian communities in the mid-40s CE; nothing external names them.

label: Paul circumcised Timothy because of the Jews, who all knew his father was Greek
statement: Paul took Timothy and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those parts, for they all knew that his father was a Greek — the son of a Jewish mother counted as Jewish and was expected to be circumcised.

label: The decrees of the apostles and elders at Jerusalem were delivered to the cities
statement: As they went through the cities, they delivered the decrees to keep, ordained by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem (the settlement of the circumcision question of Acts 15).
note: Acts 15 is not yet committed to the graph; no external source attests the delivery of the decrees.

label: Through Phrygia and Galatia, forbidden Asia, Bithynia not allowed
statement: Going through the region of Phrygia and Galatia they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia; coming opposite Mysia they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them.
note: The regions are attested; the prohibitions are an internal claim of divine guidance with none-found.

label: They came down to Troas
statement: Passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas (Alexandria Troas), the port of northwest Asia Minor.
note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

label: A vision of a Macedonian man begging 'Come over into Macedonia and help us'
statement: A vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia standing, begging him and saying, 'Come over into Macedonia and help us.'
note: Vision/miracle claim; none-found in every external category. Never graded from setting evidence.

label: From Troas a straight course to Samothrace, next day Neapolis, then to Philippi
statement: Setting sail from Troas they made a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi — the sea crossing to Europe and the land leg on the Via Egnatia.
note: The narrative 'we' section begins at 16:10-11; the voyage itself has no external witness.

label: Philippi was a city of Macedonia, where they stayed some days
statement: They came to Philippi, a city of Macedonia (named for Philip II of Macedon), and stayed some days in this city.
note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

label: Philippi was the foremost city of its district (meris) and a Roman colony
statement: Philippi is called 'the foremost city of the district' (protē tes meridos) and a Roman colony — refounded as Colonia Iulia (Augusta) Philippensis after 42 BC.
note: Disputed detail: some manuscripts read protē ('first'), others prōti ('to the first'); the western district's neighbor Amphipolis was capital of the eastern meris, so 'foremost of the district' is qualified. The colonial name Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensis rests on inscriptions reported by modern scholarship; a directly fetched inscription is still needed for an A.

label: A place of prayer (proseuchē) outside the gate by the riverside
statement: On the Sabbath they went outside the city gate by the riverside, where they supposed there was a place of prayer (proseuchē), and spoke to the women who had come together.
note: Proseuchē can denote both the act of prayer and a Jewish prayer-house; no Philippi proseuchē building has been excavated or fetched.

label: Lydia, a seller of purple from Thyatira, a worshiper of God
statement: A woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard them; the Lord opened her heart to listen to Paul.

label: Lydia and her household were baptized and the party stayed at her house
statement: Lydia and her household were baptized, and she persuaded Paul and his companions to stay at her house.
note: Conversion event; none-found externally.

label: A slave girl with a python spirit brought her masters gain by soothsaying
statement: A slave girl having a spirit of divination (pneuma pythōna, a 'python spirit') met them and brought her masters much gain by fortune-telling.
note: The 'python spirit' belongs to the world of the Pythia of Delphi and the engastrimythoi (ventriloquist soothsayers); the girl herself is not externally attested.

label: Paul commanded the spirit out in the name of Jesus Christ, and it came out that hour
statement: Paul, greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!' And it came out that very hour.
note: Miracle claim; none-found in every external category.

label: Masters seized Paul and Silas and accused them before the rulers in the marketplace
statement: Her masters, seeing their gain gone, seized Paul and Silas, dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers, and accused them to the magistrates: 'These men, being Jews, agitate our city and advocate customs not lawful for us to accept or observe, being Romans.'
note: The accusation's substance (unlawful customs for Romans) is the narrative's own report; no external source attests the charge.

label: Philippi's magistrates (strategoi) heard the case
statement: The case was brought before the city magistrates (strategoi), the Greek title corresponding to the colony's duumviri.
note: The equivalence strategoi = duumviri is modern interpretation of the Greek term in a Latin-speaking colony; the duumviral government of Philippi itself is documented.

label: The magistrates tore their clothes and ordered them beaten with rods
statement: The crowd rose up together; the magistrates tore their clothes off and commanded them to be beaten with rods (rhabdizō) — the lictors' rods.
note: Beating with rods was the colonial lictors' punishment; no Philippi-specific text or inscription of a rod beating was fetched.

label: Many stripes, the inner prison, and feet fastened in the stocks
statement: After many stripes they were thrown into prison, and the jailer, receiving the charge, threw them into the inner prison and secured their feet in the stocks (xylon).
note: No excavated Philippi prison or stocks; the traditional 'jail of Philippi' identification is late reception.

label: A great earthquake opened every door and loosened every bond
statement: Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; immediately all the doors were opened and everyone's bonds were loosened.
note: Miracle-linked event; per the brief none-found. No earthquake at Philippi c. 49-56 CE is recorded in any fetched source; no seismite or geological observation for Macedonia in that window was fetchable.

label: The jailer was about to kill himself, supposing the prisoners had escaped
statement: The jailer, roused from sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing the prisoners had escaped — the keeper of a prison answers for an escaped prisoner with his life.
note: The same legal background attested for Acts 12:18-19 (Digest 48.3.12pr: a guard who loses custody is brought into danger).

label: The magistrates sent the sergeants (rhabdouchoi, lictors) with orders to release them
statement: When it was day, the magistrates sent the sergeants (rhabdouchoi, the lictors) with the order 'Let those men go.'
note: Lictors as magistrates' rod-bearing attendants are documented generally; no Philippi-specific lictor record was fetched.

label: Roman citizens beaten publicly without trial; the magistrates must come themselves
statement: Paul protested: 'They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now they release us secretly? No indeed — let them come themselves and bring us out!' Roman citizens were protected by the Porcian laws against degrading punishment without condemnation.
note: The Lex Porciae (third century BC) exempted Roman citizens from scourging and the like; Cicero's Verrine oration (2.5) treats scourging a citizen as wickedness. Whether Paul held citizenship is his own report, not externally attested.

label: The magistrates were afraid, came and appealed to them, and brought them out
statement: The sergeants reported these words; the magistrates were afraid when they heard they were Romans, came and appealed to them, brought them out, and asked them to leave the city.
note: Their fear presupposes the citizen-protection custom; the event itself has no external witness.

label: They went into Lydia's house, encouraged the brothers, and departed
statement: They went out of the prison, entered Lydia's house, and when they had seen and encouraged the brothers, they departed — a house-church meeting at Philippi.
note: None-found externally; the Philippian assembly is later attested only by Paul's letter (biblical cross-reference).

label: The jailer washed their wounds and was baptized at once, with all his household
statement: The same hour of the night the jailer took them, washed their stripes, and was baptized immediately, he and all his household — baptism on confession without delay.
note: Conversion event; none-found externally.

label: Wikisource: Cicero, Against Verres 2.5.63 (O Porcian law!)
title: Against Verres, Second pleading, Book 5
excerpt: O the sweet name of liberty! O the admirable privileges of our citizenship! O Porcian law! O Sempronian laws!
